title: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS
blurb: A visitor from another star, crossing the picture in three hours.
story: 3I/ATLAS is only the third object ever seen passing through our Solar System from another star. SPHEREx caught it on 14 December 2025, five days before its closest approach to Earth. The fuzzy blob is the comet's cloud of gas and dust. It crosses the whole picture in 3 hours 20 minutes while the stars stay put. Try Time-lapse to watch it go.
name: Comet 3I/ATLAS on 14 Dec 2025

title: Asteroid Vesta on the move
blurb: The brightest asteroid slides past the stars in ten hours.
story: Vesta is the brightest asteroid in the sky and the second-largest body in the asteroid belt; NASA's Dawn spacecraft orbited it in 2011–12. In these pictures from 16–17 July 2026 it is the dazzling object with the halo. In ten hours it moves about 6 arcminutes, a fifth of the width of the full Moon.
name: Asteroid (4) Vesta on 16–17 Jul 2026

title: Spot the asteroid
blurb: One of these “stars” is the metal asteroid Psyche. Can you find it?
story: One of the dots in this picture is not a star. It is (16) Psyche, a metal-rich asteroid about 220 km across and the target of NASA's Psyche mission. Blink the two pictures, taken six and a half hours apart on 9 September 2025, and find the dot that moves. Then tick “Label known asteroids & comets” below to check your answer.
name: A star field in Taurus on 9 Sep 2025

title: A comet's hidden gas
blurb: The same comet in a colour where carbon dioxide glows.
story: Same comet, same three hours, a different SPHEREx detector. Every exposure records a slightly different infrared colour. At most colours here 3I/ATLAS is a faint dot, but near 4.26 µm, where carbon dioxide gas glows, it swells into a huge cloud. In this example the big change is colour, not time: play the Time-lapse and watch the wavelength in the caption.
name: Comet 3I/ATLAS at 4.0–4.3 µm, 14 Dec 2025

title: Barnard's Star
blurb: The fastest-moving star in our sky, caught a year apart.
story: Barnard's Star is a small red star only six light-years away. It crosses the sky faster than any other star: about 10 arcseconds a year. Watch the bright star in the middle step upward (north) between August 2025 and September 2026 while everything else stays still.
name: Barnard's Star

title: Epsilon Indi B
blurb: Two brown dwarfs 12 light-years away, sliding 4.7″ a year.
story: Epsilon Indi B is a pair of brown dwarfs — too small to shine like stars — circling the star Epsilon Indi, only 12 light-years from us. Because they are so close, they slide across the sky by about 4.7 arcseconds every year. Blink the first and the last visit: the dot in the middle steps toward the south-east while the stars around it stay put.
name: Epsilon Indi B

title: WISE 0855
blurb: The coldest brown dwarf known. Too faint for one exposure — until they are added up.
story: WISE 0855 is the coldest brown dwarf known: colder than ice, and only about 7 light-years away. In a single two-minute SPHEREx exposure it barely rises out of the noise. Here every visit's exposures are added together, and a faint dot appears in the cross-hair. Blink the visits: it steps toward the west, about 8 arcseconds a year. Blink X found it by itself this way.
name: WISE 0855−0714

title: RW Aurigae
blurb: A young star with unsteady light: about 60% brighter a year later.
story: RW Aurigae is a young star still pulling in gas from the disc around it, and its light is famously unsteady. Between September 2025 and September 2026 SPHEREx saw it grow about 60% brighter at these wavelengths, while the stars around it stayed the same. Blink the first and last visit, then open its doodle to see the brightness at each visit.
name: RW Aurigae

title: R Draconis
blurb: A pulsing red giant, so bright it overloads the detector.
story: R Draconis is a red giant that swells and shrinks every 245 days, and its brightness rises and falls with it. It is one of the brightest infrared stars in this part of the sky: so bright that it overloads SPHEREx's detector, which is why its middle looks blocky and long spikes run out of it. Blink X measured it against the stars around it and found changes of 10–20% between visits — too small, on an overloaded star, for it to call. No doodle here is the honest answer.
name: R Draconis

title: All five doodles (simulated)
blurb: A made-up field with a pretend Planet X, to show every doodle shape.
story: SIMULATED, not real data. Nobody has found a zigzag in SPHEREx pictures yet, so this made-up patch of sky shows what one would look like: a pretend planet 500 times farther from the Sun than Earth, jumping 14 arcminutes back and forth between four visits six months apart. The field also holds a pretend fast star, asteroid, comet and variable star. The doodles below were found by the same automatic search that runs on the real pictures.
name: Simulated field (not real sky)
